title: Build a page people can use
outcome: Create a labelled message form that works with a keyboard.
story: Amina wants customers to send a message without needing to understand her software. Give them a page with clear words, a name field, and a message field.

frames.explanation: A visible label explains the field and can be connected to it for assistive technology.

frames.action: Add the message field and action
frames.explanation: The page makes its purpose and next action clear.

sections.title: HTML gives content a structure
paragraphs: HTML describes the meaning of a page. A heading introduces its subject. A main element contains the page’s primary content. A form groups related inputs and an action.

Use elements for their intended jobs. A button is already operable with a keyboard and exposes its role to assistive technology. A clickable div requires you to recreate those behaviours and is easy to get wrong.

sections.title: Connect a label to a field
paragraphs: A label tells a person what to enter. Give the input an id and set the label’s for attribute to the same id. Clicking the label will focus its input, and assistive technology can use the label as the field’s accessible name.

A placeholder is a hint inside an empty field. It disappears after typing and is not a replacement for a visible label. Choose clear names such as Your name and Your message rather than making the person guess.

sections.title: Use browser validation deliberately
paragraphs: The required attribute marks a field as necessary. The browser can check whether required fields contain a value. A textarea is useful for a message that may span several lines.
Browser validation helps people correct a form. It does not protect the backend: a request can be sent without this page. We will validate requests again at the service boundary in lesson 15.

sections.title: Try the page without a mouse
paragraphs: Use Tab to move between the name field, message field, and button. A visible focus outline helps you know where you are. Keep the order of elements logical and avoid positive tabindex values that create a surprising order.
This lesson builds the structure and checks the fields. It does not send a real customer message yet. Lesson 10 will add behaviour, and lesson 17 will connect an interface to a backend.

words.meaning: Markup that describes the meaning and structure of a web page.
Visible text that identifies what a field is for.
Making the interface usable by people with different abilities and ways of interacting.

example.code: Contact Amina

explanation: The label’s for value matches the input id.

exercise.title: A clear contact form
exercise.brief: Build the form structure. Use the specified identifiers so the checks can inspect the real elements and their behaviour.

steps.title: Give the page a purpose
steps.task: Add an h1 saying Contact Amina and a form with id message-form inside main.

steps.title: Add connected fields
steps.task: Add a Your name label/input with id customer, and a Your message label/textarea with id message. Connect both labels using for.
steps.hint: For each field, the label’s for attribute must exactly match the field id.
steps.solution: Contact Amina

steps.title: Make the action and rules clear
steps.task: Mark both fields required and add a submit button saying Send message.
steps.hint: Use the required attribute and a native button with type="submit".
steps.solution: Contact Amina

cases.label: A clear main heading
cases.why: A person needs to know what this page does.

cases.label: Fields belong to a form
cases.why: A form groups the task and supports native submission behaviour.

cases.label: The name field has a connected label
cases.script: const field=document.getElementById("customer"); return field?.tagName==="INPUT" && field.type==="text" && field.labels?.[0]?.textContent==="Your name";
cases.why: A visible connected label works after the person starts typing.

cases.label: The message field has a connected label
cases.script: const field=document.getElementById("message"); return field?.tagName==="TEXTAREA" && field.labels?.[0]?.textContent==="Your message";
cases.why: A message needs an identified multi-line field.

cases.label: A native submit button
cases.why: The action must be clear and keyboard operable.

cases.label: Filled fields pass browser validation
cases.why: Validation should also allow intended success.

project.title: A customer message page
project.brief: Create a standalone, semantic contact page with visible labels and a logical keyboard order. State that it is a practice form until a backend is connected.
deliverables: An HTML page with the contact form.
A list of browser and backend validation responsibilities.

milestones.title: Build the structure
actions: Add main, a heading, and a form.

milestones.title: Connect the fields
actions: Add required rules and the action button.

milestones.title: Try another way to use it
actions: Click each label to focus its field.

acceptance: The purpose is clear from the heading.
Both fields have visible connected labels.
The action is a native button.
Keyboard navigation and focus are usable.
The page does not claim to send a real message yet.

tests.expected: Name, message, and action follow a logical order.
Browser validation asks for the missing values.

project.extension: Add a labelled email field and explain what the browser can check versus what the backend must still verify.
reflection: Why is a placeholder not enough?
How did you check keyboard use?
Why will the backend still need validation?
